---
title: "Setting Up Your Environment"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Setting Up Your Environment"
  description-meta: "What to install, how tidy tables and date-indexed return matrices coexist in R, and how to read the code in every chapter of this book."
---



What has to be installed, and in what shape must a return series arrive, before
any portfolio in this book can be computed? The second question has two
canonical answers that do not agree: @wickham2014 defined a tidy table as one
observation per row and one variable per column, and @zeileis2005 built the
ordered, date-indexed matrix that `zoo` and `xts` carry and that every
optimization function in `PortfolioAnalytics` expects. Both are used in every
chapter of this book, and the boundary between them is crossed each time data
are prepared for an optimizer or read back out of one, so we fix it here, once.

We first list what to install and what each package is for, then set out the
two data models and why neither can be given up, then cross the boundary
between them on the book's own data and break it in the three ways it breaks,
and finally read the data once in the way every later chapter will. On the
horizon axis that @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory defines, this
chapter is neither strategic nor tactical: it allocates nothing.

Three programs come first: R, of which the book was built on
4.6.1 and anything from 4.4
onward will do; an editor, RStudio or Visual Studio Code with the R extension;
and Quarto [@allaire2022], needed only to render the book's source, not to run
its code. The packages install from CRAN in one call.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "xts", "zoo",                                  # data models
  "PortfolioAnalytics", "PerformanceAnalytics",               # the subject
  "ROI", "ROI.plugin.quadprog", "ROI.plugin.glpk", "quadprog", # convex solvers
  "osqp", "CVXR", "DEoptim", "GenSA", "pso",                  # more solvers
  "corpcor", "renv"                                           # shrinkage, pinning
))
```
:::


The companion package `tidypm` is not on CRAN. It holds the modeled market
of @sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, the two coercion functions this
chapter is about, and the machinery that `PortfolioAnalytics` does not cover,
recorded in @sec-93-package-notes; it installs from GitHub.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pak::pak("sstoeckl/tidypm")
```
:::


`renv.lock` records every version the book was built against, and `renv`
[@ushey2026] restores that record, so that the printed numbers reproduce to
the last digit rather than to whatever CRAN offers on the day.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
renv::restore()
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::

The tidyverse [@wickham2019] is the data-manipulation half of @tbl-01-packages,
with @wickham2023 as its reference; `xts` [@ryan2026] on top of `zoo`
[@zeileis2005] is the time-series half. `PortfolioAnalytics` [@peterson2026]
and `PerformanceAnalytics` [@peterson2026a] are the subject and its engine.
The solvers are backends that `PortfolioAnalytics` dispatches to by name:
`ROI` [@theussl2020] for quadratic and linear programs, `CVXR` [@fu2020] for
convex problems `ROI` cannot express, and `DEoptim` [@ardia2011], `GenSA` and
`pso` for problems that are not convex at all. @sec-13-solvers-theory says
which to use when, and @sec-92-solver-matrix tables which constraint each
supports.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two functions for everything, and none for data

`PortfolioAnalytics` exports more names than it has functions.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
exports <- getNamespaceExports("PortfolioAnalytics")
legacy  <- sort(grep("_v[12]", exports, value = TRUE))
c(exports = length(exports), legacy = length(legacy))
#> exports  legacy 
#>     115      14
legacy
#>  [1] "add.objective_v1"                  "add.objective_v2"                 
#>  [3] "constrained_objective_v1"          "constrained_objective_v2"         
#>  [5] "constraint_v1"                     "constraint_v2"                    
#>  [7] "optimize.portfolio.rebalancing_v1" "optimize.portfolio_v1"            
#>  [9] "optimize.portfolio_v2"             "random_portfolios_v1"             
#> [11] "random_portfolios_v2"              "randomize_portfolio_v1"           
#> [13] "randomize_portfolio_v2"            "update_constraint_v1tov2"
```
:::


14 of the 115 exports carry a `_v1` or `_v2`
suffix. They are the interface of an earlier generation of the package, kept
so that old scripts keep running, and they are why an answer copied from an
old forum post fails against the current release. The unsuffixed
`add.objective()`, `add.constraint()` and `optimize.portfolio()` are the
package; this book uses only those.



The other absence is data. Of the 115 exports,
none fetch anything, and the package
bundles 1 dataset,
`indexes`. It optimizes what it is
handed, and handing it the right object is the subject of this chapter.
:::

## Two Data Models {#sec-01-setting-up-theory}

A return panel is a set of numbers indexed by a date and an asset, and there
are two ways to lay it out, each of which makes some operations natural and
others awkward.

The **tidy** layout of @wickham2014 stores one observation per row: a date, an
asset identifier and a return. A panel of $N$ assets over $T$ periods is a
table of $TN$ rows and three columns, and every operation of relational
algebra applies to it directly: a sub-period is a filter on the date, a
universe is a filter on the asset, a currency return or a yield is a join on
the keys, and a computation that runs asset by asset is a grouped mutate.
That is how the real data sleeves of @sec-02-notation-and-data-real-data are
assembled, how the screens of @sec-20-sustainability-implementation are
applied, and how every figure in the book is prepared, since `ggplot2`
consumes long data and nothing else.

The **wide** layout stores the same panel as a $T \times N$ matrix with the
dates as an ordered index and the assets as named columns. In the notation that
@sec-02-notation-and-data-notation fixes,

$$
\boldsymbol{R} =
\begin{pmatrix}
r_{1,1} & \cdots & r_{1,N} \\
\vdots  &        & \vdots  \\
r_{T,1} & \cdots & r_{T,N}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{r}_t' = (r_{t,1}, \dots, r_{t,N}),
$$ {#eq-01-matrix}

where $\boldsymbol{r}_t$ is row $t$, the cross-section of returns on date $t$.
A portfolio with weight vector $\boldsymbol{w}$ earns

$$
r_{p,t} = \boldsymbol{r}_t'\boldsymbol{w} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\, r_{t,i},
$$ {#eq-01-portfolio-return}

and the sample moments that @sec-09-mean-variance-theory optimizes over are
matrix expressions in $\boldsymbol{R}$ and the vector of ones
$\boldsymbol{\iota}$:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \frac{1}{T}\,\boldsymbol{R}'\boldsymbol{\iota},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \frac{1}{T-1}
  \left(\boldsymbol{R} - \boldsymbol{\iota}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\right)'
  \left(\boldsymbol{R} - \boldsymbol{\iota}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\right).
$$ {#eq-01-moments}

`zoo` [@zeileis2005] made this layout a first-class object in R by attaching
an ordered index to a matrix, and `xts` [@ryan2026] specialized it to time, so
that subsetting by date range, aligning two series, changing the frequency and
rolling a window are each one call. Every function in `PortfolioAnalytics`
and `PerformanceAnalytics` takes this object and nothing else; there is no
method for a data frame.

Neither layout can be dropped: the long table is where data are built,
because joining, filtering and grouping are relational operations and a matrix
has no join, and the wide matrix is where portfolios are computed, because
@eq-01-matrix through @eq-01-moments are matrix expressions. The boundary is
therefore crossed in a fixed direction, long to wide once after the panel is
built, wide to long whenever a result is to be drawn. `timetk` and `tsibble`
hide the crossing; the book does not use them, because an explicit crossing
can be checked.

The three equations also say what can go wrong, before any code does. In
@eq-01-matrix, $T$ is one number shared by every column, so a panel in which
one asset is missing a date has no matrix representation until the gap is
filled or the date is dropped, and either choice changes @eq-01-moments. In
@eq-01-portfolio-return, the $i$ that indexes $w_i$ and the $i$ that indexes
$r_{t,i}$ must be the same asset, which a matrix product enforces by position
and nothing else. And the map from $(t, i)$ to $r_{t,i}$ must be a function: a
panel in which some $(t, i)$ appears twice describes no matrix at all. These
are the three failure modes of the boundary, and @sec-01-setting-up-implementation
produces each from the book's data.

## The Tibble–xts Boundary {#sec-01-setting-up-implementation}

`tidypm` provides the crossing in both directions. `as_xts_pm()` takes a long
table and the names of its date, identifier and value columns and returns the
matrix of @eq-01-matrix; `as_pm()` takes the matrix back to three columns.
The book's data ship in the long form.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sim_class_returns_monthly |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   date       class          return index
#>   <date>     <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2101-01-31 CH_credit     -0.0301  97.0
#> 2 2101-01-31 CH_equity     -0.0145  98.6
#> 3 2101-01-31 CH_government -0.0343  96.6
#> 4 2101-01-31 EU_credit     -0.0241  97.6
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, nrow(R) == length(rf), !anyNA(R),
          all(zoo::index(R) == sim_riskfree_monthly$date))
```
:::


The assertions state what the rest of the chapter assumes about `R`; if any
of them were false the chunk would fail here, naming the condition, rather
than three chapters later with a plausible number.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
few <- c("US_equity", "US_government", "GLOBAL_commodity")
head(R[, few], 3)
#>            US_equity US_government GLOBAL_commodity
#> 2101-01-31  0.025013     -0.017372          0.02562
#> 2101-02-28  0.022790     -0.006756         -0.02290
#> 2101-03-31  0.005306     -0.003734         -0.02316
```
:::


The reverse crossing returns a tibble with exactly three columns, and going
round the loop changes nothing.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tb <- as_pm(R)
tb
#> # A tibble: 5,952 × 3
#>    date       asset               value
#>    <date>     <chr>               <dbl>
#>  1 2101-01-31 CH_credit        -0.0301 
#>  2 2101-01-31 CH_equity        -0.0145 
#>  3 2101-01-31 CH_government    -0.0343 
#>  4 2101-01-31 EU_credit        -0.0241 
#>  5 2101-01-31 EU_equity         0.0837 
#>  6 2101-01-31 EU_government    -0.0188 
#>  7 2101-01-31 GLOBAL_commodity  0.0256 
#>  8 2101-01-31 JP_credit         0.00347
#>  9 2101-01-31 JP_equity        -0.0388 
#> 10 2101-01-31 JP_government     0.0141 
#> # ℹ 5,942 more rows
stopifnot(identical(zoo::coredata(as_xts_pm(tb, date, asset, value)),
                    zoo::coredata(R)))
```
:::


### Three ways the boundary breaks

Each failure below is manufactured from `sim_class_returns_monthly`, so that
the message the reader will meet in practice is printed here first.

**A ragged panel.** Drop one row, the
EU_equity observation for
2101-01-31, and cross the boundary.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ragged <- sim_class_returns_monthly[-5, ]

R_ragged <- withCallingHandlers(
  as_xts_pm(ragged, date, class, return),
  warning = function(w) { cat(conditionMessage(w), "\n"); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }
)
#> Padded 1 missing return with "NA".
#> ℹ PortfolioAnalytics will not warn about these, but they change the effective
#>   sample of every moment estimate.
#> → Handle the gaps before crossing the boundary.

na_at <- which(is.na(R_ragged), arr.ind = TRUE)
c(row = as.character(zoo::index(R_ragged))[na_at[, "row"]],
  column = colnames(R_ragged)[na_at[, "col"]])
#>          row       column 
#> "2101-01-31"  "EU_equity"
```
:::


The coercion pads rather than refuses, and says so. Two consequences follow.
The first is that EU_equity has moved from
column 5 to column
16, because `as_xts_pm()` orders
columns by first appearance in the table and the dropped row was that asset's
first appearance. The second is what an optimizer does with the gap. For a
variance objective, `set.portfolio.moments()` estimates the mean with
`na.rm = TRUE` and the covariance with `use = "pairwise.complete.obs"`, so
one column is estimated on 371 months and the
other fifteen on 372, and the matrix that
results is the covariance of no sample that exists. The minimum-variance
problem below is the one @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation builds up
properly; here it only shows that the optimizer accepts the padded matrix
without comment.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_of <- function(x) {
  portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(x)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}
w_full   <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(R,        spec_of(R),        optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_ragged <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(R_ragged, spec_of(R_ragged), optimize_method = "ROI"))

w_ragged <- w_ragged[names(w_full)]            # index by name: the columns moved
max_shift <- max(abs(w_ragged - w_full))
round(c(largest_weight_change = max_shift, cells_missing = sum(is.na(R_ragged))), 4)
#> largest_weight_change         cells_missing 
#>                0.0027                1.0000
```
:::


The weights move by at most 0.0027, small because one
month in 372 is small; the same gap in the sixty-month windows of
@sec-25-backtesting-implementation is one month in sixty, and a sleeve of
instruments that list and delist, the setting of @sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory,
is ragged by construction. The warning is the only notice the reader gets, and
it comes from the coercion, not the optimizer. Handle the gap in the long
table, before crossing.

**Column order.** The sort order of the long table becomes the column order of
the matrix. Sort it differently, as a join or a `dplyr::arrange()` might, and
the columns come out in a different order, from the same numbers.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
reordered <- sim_class_returns_monthly |> dplyr::arrange(date, dplyr::desc(class))
R_rev     <- as_xts_pm(reordered, date, class, return)

c(same_set = setequal(colnames(R), colnames(R_rev)),
  same_order = identical(colnames(R), colnames(R_rev)))
#>   same_set same_order 
#>       TRUE      FALSE
colnames(R_rev)[1:3]
#> [1] "US_government" "US_equity"     "US_credit"
```
:::


Now take a weight vector built in the original order, a 60/40 portfolio of
`US_equity` and `US_government`, and apply it to the reordered matrix.
`Return.portfolio()` pairs weights with columns by position.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w <- setNames(numeric(ncol(R)), colnames(R))
w[c("US_equity", "US_government")] <- c(0.6, 0.4)

rp <- merge(PerformanceAnalytics::Return.portfolio(R_rev, weights = w),
            PerformanceAnalytics::Return.portfolio(R_rev[, names(w)], weights = w))
colnames(rp) <- c("positional", "by_name")
PerformanceAnalytics::table.AnnualizedReturns(rp, Rf = rf)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   positional by_name
#>        <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1     0.0938   0.114
#> 2     0.150    0.130
#> 3     0.464    0.692
```
:::


The positional column is a portfolio of
CH_equity and CH_credit, because those
are the series that now occupy the positions the weights were written for, and
nothing reports that it is the wrong one. The guard is the condition of
@eq-01-portfolio-return, that the index of the weights and the index of the
columns are the same index:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tryCatch(stopifnot(identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w))),
         error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
#> Error: identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w)) is not TRUE

w <- w[colnames(R_rev)]                          # reindex by name, then assert
stopifnot(identical(colnames(R_rev), names(w)))
```
:::


The same discipline applies coming out of the optimizer. `extractWeights()`
returns a named vector in the column order of the matrix it was fitted on, and
a vector fitted on one ordering and applied by position to another mis-pairs
every entry.

**Duplicate keys.** If a date–asset pair appears twice, the table describes no
matrix, and the failure surfaces in two steps.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dup <- dplyr::bind_rows(sim_class_returns_monthly,
                        dplyr::slice_head(sim_class_returns_monthly, n = 1))

tryCatch(
  withCallingHandlers(
    as_xts_pm(dup, date, class, return),
    warning = function(w) { cat("Warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n"); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }),
  error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
#> Warning: Values from `return` are not uniquely identified; output will contain
#> list-cols.
#> • Use `values_fn = list` to suppress this warning.
#> • Use `values_fn = {summary_fun}` to summarise duplicates.
#> • Use the following dplyr code to identify duplicates.
#>   {data} |>
#>   dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(date, class)) |>
#>   dplyr::filter(n > 1L) 
#> Error: cannot convert lists to xts objects
```
:::


The warning comes from `tidyr::pivot_wider()` and names the cause; the error
comes from `xts()` and names only the symptom, and a reader who sees the error
alone has no way back to the duplicated pair. The check belongs before the
crossing, in the long table, where the keys are columns:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dup |> dplyr::count(date, class) |> dplyr::filter(n > 1)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   date       class         n
#>   <date>     <chr>     <int>
#> 1 2101-01-31 CH_credit     2
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(sim_class_returns_monthly[c("date", "class")]))
```
:::


These three chunks are the first appearance of a rule the book applies
wherever two objects have to line up and nothing in the language enforces it:
state the invariant as an assertion that fails the render, not as a comment.
Index by name, then assert that the names agree. The rule recurs in
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, where weight vectors are indexed against
the columns of the return matrix and group limits against the output of
`split()`, and in @sec-25-backtesting-implementation, where a rolling
optimization that fails in one window must not enter the record as a portfolio
that did not move.

## A First Pass Through the Data {#sec-01-setting-up-application}

### How the code in this book is written

Every chapter opens with the same lines, run from the project root.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/_common.R")                                              # seed, options, theme
library(tidypm)                                                    # the market, the boundary
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the Treasury bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
```
:::


`R/_common.R` attaches the tidyverse, `xts` and the two analytics packages,
sets the seed to 1602, sets the printing options, registers `theme_tidyaa()`
as the default `ggplot2` theme with the palette `tidyaa_colors` and the scale
`scale_colour_tidyaa()`, and warns if the installed `PortfolioAnalytics` is
not the build the lockfile records (@sec-93-package-notes). The data then load
in two lines and a third subtracts the bill
(@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory); no chapter prepares data beyond
this.

Three conventions follow. Every number in the prose is computed inline from an
object a chunk created, never typed. Every figure is built from one long data
frame, one row per plotted thing, so that an $x$ cannot be paired with another
row's $y$; that frame is usually the output of `as_pm()`. And `ggplot2`'s
`colour` argument keeps its spelling in code while the prose is American. A
reader who has not written R recently will find the language itself in
@sec-94-r-primer.

### The shape of the data

The matrix built above is what @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-theory describes
and every chapter after it consumes, so its dimensions are worth reading once.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- xts::periodicity(R)
c(months = nrow(R), assets = ncol(R),
  from = as.character(start(R)), to = as.character(end(R)), scale = p$scale)
#>       months       assets         from           to        scale 
#>        "372"         "16" "2101-01-31" "2131-12-31"    "monthly"
```
:::


372 months of 16 series, from
2101-01 to 2131-12,
31 years on a monthly grid. A figure of three of them shows
the reverse crossing in use: the matrix goes back to long form, a grouped
mutate compounds each series, and the plot is drawn from that one frame.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
growth <- as_pm(R[, few]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(asset) |>
  dplyr::mutate(growth = cumprod(1 + value)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

ggplot2::ggplot(growth, ggplot2::aes(date, growth, colour = asset)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "growth of one dollar, log scale", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tidyaa()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Growth of one dollar in three of the sixteen series, on a log scale. Built from one long data frame, one row per date and asset, the shape as_pm() returns.](01-setting-up_files/figure-html/fig-01-growth-1.png){#fig-01-growth fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::




Later chapters omit the call to `theme_tidyaa()`, which `R/_common.R` has
already set. One dollar in `US_equity` at the start of the sample is
44.6 dollars at the end, against
4.0 in `US_government` and
4.1 in `GLOBAL_commodity`.


::: {#tbl-01-annualized .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Annualized return, volatility and Sharpe ratio for three series, from PerformanceAnalytics on the wide matrix. The bill enters as a vector aligned with the rows.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
PerformanceAnalytics::table.AnnualizedReturns(R[, few], Rf = rf) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|                             | US_equity| US_government| GLOBAL_commodity|
|:----------------------------|---------:|-------------:|----------------:|
|Annualized Return            |     0.130|         0.045|            0.046|
|Annualized Std Dev           |     0.156|         0.048|            0.140|
|Annualized Sharpe (Rf=2.24%) |     0.676|         0.469|            0.166|


:::
:::


The function annualizes the bill itself and prints the rate it used. The
return in the first row is compounded and the Sharpe ratio divides the excess
over the bill by the volatility; @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-theory fixes these
conventions for the book and says where the arithmetic mean is used instead.

### Reproducibility

Three things are pinned so that a reader's numbers match the printed ones: the
seed, set once in `R/_common.R`; the 299 package versions in
`renv.lock`, with `freeze: auto` in `_quarto.yml` so that a chapter is
re-executed only when its source changes; and the modeled market, at dataset
version 6.2.0. The last pin is the one to respect most, because the source
model redraws its idiosyncratic components on every run, so a regenerated
dataset is a different realized path rather than a refresh;
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market explains why regenerating it is an
event. The text is executed by `knitr` [@xie2015] and assembled by Quarto
[@allaire2022], the arrangement of the two books this one sits beside,
@scheuch2023 and @coqueret2020, and for the same reason: a number the reader
cannot recompute is a number the reader cannot check.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- Two data models are unavoidable. The tidy long table of @wickham2014 is
  where a return panel is built, filtered and joined; the date-indexed matrix
  of @zeileis2005 and `xts` is what every function in `PortfolioAnalytics` and
  `PerformanceAnalytics` consumes, and it is the $\boldsymbol{R}$ of
  @eq-01-matrix.
- The boundary is crossed in a fixed direction, one call each way:
  `as_xts_pm()` from long to wide, once, after the panel is built; `as_pm()`
  from wide to long whenever a result is to be drawn.
- The boundary fails in three ways, none reported downstream: a ragged panel
  is padded and each moment is then estimated on a different sample; a
  differently sorted table gives a differently ordered matrix, so weights
  applied by position land on the wrong assets; a duplicated key fails with an
  error that names only the symptom.
- The guard is the same in every case: index by name, then assert that the
  names agree, with a `stopifnot()` that fails the render.
- The `_v1` and `_v2` exports of `PortfolioAnalytics` are legacy shims; the
  book uses the unsuffixed functions. The package fetches no data and
  optimizes what it is given.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. The five money-market series ship beside the universe as
   `sim_money_market_monthly`. Bring them across the boundary and attach them
   to `R` with `merge()`, then confirm that the result has 21 columns, 372
   rows and no `NA`. Do the same in the long form, with `dplyr::bind_rows()`
   before a single call to `as_xts_pm()`. Which route makes the alignment
   check unnecessary, and why?
2. Remove every `JP_equity` row from the first three model years from
   `sim_class_returns_monthly` and cross the boundary. Report the number of
   observations per column, then compute the covariance matrix with
   `use = "complete.obs"` and with `use = "pairwise.complete.obs"` and count
   the entries that differ. Check whether the pairwise matrix is positive
   definite from its smallest eigenvalue. Which of the two would
   `PortfolioAnalytics` have used?
3. For each of the legacy exports listed in the callout above, determine
   whether an unsuffixed function of the same name exists in the namespace.
   Which shims have no modern counterpart, and what does the name
   `update_constraint_v1tov2()` say about how the constraint interface
   changed?
